title: The Negotiation

jokes.text: Karen calls Jim 'agoraphobic' for preferring to watch a Phillies game on the couch over going out
jokes.setup: Karen frames Jim's preference for staying home as a psychological disorder
jokes.punchline: Jim immediately and cheerfully confirms: 'Absolutely correct.'
jokes.explanation: Jim's cheerful agreement with an unflattering diagnosis is a clean character beat — it's recognizably him. Not exceptional but efficiently sets up the domestic dynamic before the chaos hits.

jokes.text: Roy charges at Jim in the office and Dwight pepper sprays him — the sound and chaos inferred from 'Roy! Ahh! Roy, don't! God!'
jokes.setup: Normal goodbye scene at the end of the workday; Roy enters with sudden rage
jokes.punchline: Dwight — the perennial office joke — actually uses his weapons and saves Jim
jokes.explanation: Earns its high score because of masterful character payoff: Dwight has been mocked for years for his paranoid preparedness, and the show finally vindicates him in a genuinely dramatic-then-hilarious way. The comedy comes entirely from character logic built over seasons. On rewatch, this moment is even richer.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Every day for eight years, I have brought pepper spray into this office to protect myself and my fellow employees. And every day for eight years, people have laughed at me. Well. Who's laughing now?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been the office punchline for his survivalist preparedness for the entire run of the show
jokes.punchline: 'Well. Who's laughing now?' — delivered with maximum Dwight self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: One of the great Dwight moments. The comedy is entirely earned through seasons of setup — his obsessive, mocked paranoia pays off here with perfect economy. 'Well. Who's laughing now?' is maximally quotable and the beat before it (the pause implied by 'Well.') is textbook comedic timing. A genuine 8+ moment: it functions as both a laugh line and a character vindication.

jokes.text: Michael: 'It was a crime of passion, Jan, not a disgruntled employee. Everyone here is extremely gruntled.'
jokes.setup: Jan asks Michael about the attack using the word 'disgruntled' as serious HR framing
jokes.punchline: Michael mishears/misuses the word, coining 'extremely gruntled' as if it's a real word
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Michael Scott joke. 'Gruntled' is technically a real word (to be pleased), which adds a layer for the clever viewer, but Michael clearly doesn't know that — he's confidently inventing language to reassure his boss mid-crisis. It's original, efficient, deeply in-character, and has entered common pop-culture usage. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jan asks if Toby is there; Michael says 'No.' Toby quietly says 'I'm here, Jan.' — Michael has denied Toby's existence to Jan
jokes.setup: Michael tells Jan Toby is not there, presumably wanting to exclude him
jokes.punchline: Toby immediately announces himself, exposing Michael's lie in the most defeated possible way
jokes.explanation: Works beautifully as a compression of Michael's contempt for Toby and Toby's total defeat. The 'Wh-what is the situation, Toby?' from Jan immediately after is the perfect beat — Jan pretends nothing happened. Good structure, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Michael says 'Yeppers.' Jan: 'What did I tell you about yeppers?' Michael: 'I don't remember.' Jan: 'I told you not to say it. Do you remember that?' Michael: 'Ye--sh.'
jokes.setup: Michael uses 'Yeppers' in a professional crisis call with his boss
jokes.punchline: He almost says 'Yeppers' again when asked if he remembers being told not to, catching himself at 'Ye--sh'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant escalating structure: Michael uses the forbidden word, gets called out, and nearly uses it again in the same breath confirming he's been told not to. The 'Ye--sh' self-correction is physically funny even as audio — you can see it. Perfect economy. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'I really don't want to talk about it... I just don't want to comment on what happened.'
jokes.setup: Jim was just nearly assaulted at work
jokes.punchline: His refusal to discuss it is played completely straight — maximum British-style understatement about a violent incident
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Jim's refusal to engage with drama is on-brand. Works as a palette cleanser after the chaos but isn't especially clever or memorable.

jokes.text: Pam's talking head: 'It sucked.' — one word summary of the attack
jokes.setup: Serious violence just occurred in part because of Pam's romantic situation
jokes.punchline: Her entire emotional processing of the event is two words, delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy. The joke is entirely in the contrast between the enormity of what happened and the absolute minimalism of Pam's response. Functionally very funny, especially in the mockumentary format where you expect more processing.

jokes.text: Jim's second talking head: 'I guess... all things considered... I was lucky Dwight was there.'
jokes.setup: Jim has to acknowledge that Dwight — his perennial target of pranks — literally saved his life
jokes.punchline: The halting, reluctant delivery of 'I was lucky Dwight was there' — the longest emotional journey to a simple sentence
jokes.explanation: Works because of years of Jim/Dwight dynamic. The ellipses in the line ARE the joke — Jim can barely get the words out. It's a character comedy moment that requires the full context of their relationship to land.

jokes.text: Jim: 'And Roy was lucky that Dwight only used pepper spray, and not the nunchucks or the throwing stars.'
jokes.setup: Jim grudgingly acknowledges Dwight's heroism
jokes.punchline: Reveals that Dwight had multiple escalating weapons available — nunchucks, throwing stars — making the pepper spray seem like the restrained option
jokes.explanation: A very good escalation joke — pepper spray is already extreme for an office, so the revelation that it was the mildest option Dwight had is a clean absurdist escalation. Delivered with Jim's characteristic dry detachment.

jokes.text: Jim tries to thank Dwight; Dwight: 'Thank you not necessary, and thus not accepted.'
jokes.setup: Jim sincerely approaches Dwight to thank him for saving his life
jokes.punchline: Dwight refuses the thanks in a bizarrely formal, almost robotic triple structure
jokes.explanation: Dwight's refusal of thanks using bureaucratic logic ('not necessary, and thus not accepted') is a distillation of his character. The follow-up 'I saw someone breaking the law, and I interceded' is equally perfect — all duty, no emotion. Strong character integration score justified.

jokes.text: Jim presents a gift; Dwight: 'Don't want it. Won't open it. Don't need it. Won't take it. Citizens do not accept prizes for being citizens.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to give Dwight a thank-you gift
jokes.punchline: Dwight refuses in a four-part escalating declaration, culminating in an absurd philosophical principle about civic duty
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of 'Don't want it. Won't open it. Don't need it. Won't take it.' is almost poetic in its stubbornness — four short declaratives that build perfectly. Then 'Citizens do not accept prizes for being citizens' is a genuine philosophical absurdity that only Dwight could utter with full sincerity. High quotability, strong structure. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head about real heroes: 'The guys who wake up every morning and go into their normal jobs, and get a distress call from the commissioner, and take off their glasses and change into capes, and fly around fighting crime. Those are the real heroes.'
jokes.setup: Dwight begins with a humble-sounding 'don't call me a hero' setup, gesturing toward genuine heroism
jokes.punchline: He describes superheroes — with complete sincerity — as 'normal job' workers who happen to fight crime
jokes.explanation: This is Dwight at his most perfectly absurd. The setup mirrors genuine humility rhetoric ('don't call me a hero, the real heroes are...'), then pivots to a description of literal superheroes treated as blue-collar workers. The specificity — 'get a distress call from the commissioner,' 'take off their glasses' — makes it funnier. Only Dwight could deliver this with total earnestness. Deserves 8+.

jokes.text: Andy recounts the Roy fight with breathless excitement: 'All of a sudden — bam! Roy goes down, and Dwight's standing there like an action hero.'
jokes.setup: Andy witnesses (or heard about) the attack and is recounting it
jokes.punchline: His dramatic, reverent retelling treats Dwight as a genuine action movie star
jokes.explanation: Andy's fanboyish retelling is functional humor — the comedy is in his enthusiasm — but it's not doing anything exceptionally clever. Serviceable setup for the ongoing Dwight heroism thread.

jokes.text: Michael explaining his negotiation research: 'Wikipedia is the best thing ever. Anyone in the world can write anything they want about any subject. So you know you are getting the best possible information.'
jokes.setup: Michael is preparing for a serious salary negotiation using research
jokes.punchline: His description of Wikipedia perfectly inverts its actual flaw — the crowdsourced nature he cites as a quality is precisely what makes it unreliable
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp joke that works on multiple levels. Michael's confidence is total; his logic is a perfect inversion of sound reasoning; and the observation about Wikipedia was timely and specific in 2007 without feeling like a cheap reference. The structure is airtight: setup as endorsement, punchline hidden inside the endorsement itself. Highly quotable, earns 8+.

jokes.text: Michael demonstrates 'dominant physical position' in negotiation: leaning back and whispering so quietly that Dwight (playing Darryl) literally cannot hear him
jokes.setup: Michael is demonstrating Wikipedia-sourced negotiation tactics on Dwight
jokes.punchline: The 'dominant' tactic makes Michael completely inaudible — the opposite of commanding
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — Michael's 'dominant' strategy renders him powerless by its own execution. The self-defeating nature of his tactics is classic Michael. Works better as a visual moment than on the page.

jokes.text: Dwight's clinical retelling of the pepper spray incident: 'I removed my weapon from its secure hiding place. Discharged it at a distance of a little over a meter, rendering him utterly and completely disabled. The end.'
jokes.setup: Kelly asks Dwight to recount the heroic fight
jokes.punchline: Dwight narrates it like a military incident report, ending with the completely flat 'The end.'
jokes.explanation: 'The end.' is the perfect button. Dwight treats narrative storytelling as a technical debrief, stripping all drama from a genuinely dramatic moment. 'Utterly and completely disabled' followed by 'The end.' is beautiful in its bluntness. High character integration — this is unmistakably Dwight.

jokes.text: Kelly's story about Ryan being scared of a murderer in his apartment and calling her at night — Ryan's attempt to reframe: 'I call you in the middle of the night to tell you that I love you.'
jokes.setup: Kelly is publicly humiliating Ryan by revealing he calls her terrified in the night
jokes.punchline: Ryan desperately reframes a fear-call as a love-call — while noting 'there's a bunch of people back there maybe'
jokes.explanation: Ryan's transparent save — 'I call you to tell you that I love you' — is a great character beat. His cool-guy persona crumbling in real time is central to his arc. The awareness that people are nearby ('Guys?') adds a nice layer of public shame.

jokes.text: Ryan's talking head: 'I don't think Michael intended to punish me by putting Ryan back here with Kelly. But if he did intend that... wow. Genius.'
jokes.setup: Ryan has been moved back to sit next to Kelly, his controlling ex-girlfriend
jokes.punchline: Ryan can't decide if it was intentional punishment — and if it was, he's genuinely impressed
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Genius.' is the joke — Ryan's grudging admiration for a punishment this perfectly targeted. The beat works well in the talking-head format, with Ryan's pause doing visual comedy work.

jokes.text: Michael changes the meeting location from his office to the conference room, then back, then to the conference room again — frantic indecision visible in the staging
jokes.setup: Michael is using Wikipedia negotiation tactic #6: change the location at the last second
jokes.punchline: He changes it multiple times in rapid succession, destroying any tactical advantage and just being chaotic
jokes.explanation: The visual comedy of Michael flip-flopping locations while pretending it's tactical is strong physical humor. Works best as a sight gag — Michael's confusion defeating his own strategy.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head explaining tactic #6: 'Change the location of the meeting at the last second. Totally throws 'em off.'
jokes.setup: We've just watched Michael do this multiple times chaotically
jokes.punchline: His serene explanation presents this as controlled strategy when we've seen it was pure confusion
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary structure: show us the embarrassing reality, cut to the character explaining it as competence. Functional but not distinguished.

jokes.text: Michael employs tactic #14 — declining to speak first — resulting in a long, excruciating silent standoff with Darryl that Darryl breaks effortlessly
jokes.setup: Michael intends to use silence as a power move
jokes.punchline: Darryl waits, unbothered, then just starts talking normally — the silence only tortured Michael
jokes.explanation: The extended silence is a pure cringe comedy beat — Michael's tactic backfires because Darryl is simply more comfortable with silence. The visual of two men staring at each other is mined well. Darryl's unfazed 'Okay, I'll start' is the perfect non-reaction.

jokes.text: Talking-head insert: 'Number 14. Declining to speak first. Makes them feel uncomfortable, puts you in control.' — followed by extended silence in the conference room.
jokes.setup: Michael explains tactic #14 to camera — refusing to speak first
jokes.punchline: The resulting silence is prolonged and Darryl immediately fills it without discomfort, defeating the tactic
jokes.explanation: Strong structure: explain the tactic, show the tactic, show the tactic failing instantly. The comedy is in how thoroughly unintimidated Darryl is. He simply starts talking, leaving Michael's power move with no effect whatsoever.

jokes.text: Mid-negotiation, Darryl notices Michael's pants: 'Are you wearing lady clothes?' Michael: 'No, this is a power suit.' Darryl: 'That there's a woman's suit.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been conducting a serious negotiation in what turns out to be a woman's suit from a bin
jokes.punchline: Darryl derails the entire negotiation to clock Michael's outfit
jokes.explanation: The timing of the reveal — deep into a negotiation Michael is already losing — is excellent. Darryl calling it a 'woman's suit' with zero hesitation while Michael insists 'power suit' is a great character clash. The derailing of the negotiation by this observation is wonderfully absurd.

jokes.text: Michael's defense: 'I do not buy women's clothes. Would not make that mistake again.'
jokes.setup: Michael is denying that his suit is women's clothing
jokes.punchline: 'Would not make that mistake again' — implying he has made this mistake before
jokes.explanation: One of the best throwaway lines in the episode. The addition of 'again' opens up an entire undisclosed backstory in five words. Perfect economy. Steve Carell's delivery presumably lands this as a huge laugh.

jokes.text: Michael explains the suit: 'I got this out of a bin. There were these huge bins of clothes, and everybody was rifling through them like crazy, and I grabbed one. And it fit. So I don't think that is totally just a woman's suit. At the very least it's bisexual.'
jokes.setup: Michael is pressed to explain why he's wearing a woman's suit
jokes.punchline: 'At the very least it's bisexual' — Michael invents a garment sexuality classification system
jokes.explanation: The pivot from defensive explanation ('And it fit') to the completely absurd category of 'bisexual' suit is inspired. Michael is so committed to not admitting the suit is women's clothing that he invents a new taxonomy. The escalation from defensiveness to absurdism is Michael's comedic wheelhouse. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Pam confirms the suit is women's clothing; the label is revealed: 'MISSterious.' Michael: 'And it is mysterious, because the buttons are on the wrong side. That's the mystery.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is examining Michael's suit for proof it's women's clothing
jokes.punchline: The brand name 'MISSterious' is revealed; Michael immediately tries to spin the name as referencing only button placement
jokes.explanation: The brand name is a perfect prop-joke gift — 'MISSterious' screams women's brand — and Michael's desperate reinterpretation of 'mysterious' as referring to button placement is a great example of his denial logic. 'That's the mystery' is a wonderful button.

jokes.text: The group catalogs the suit's features: shoulder pads, fancy lining, no pockets. Michael: 'No, they don't. See?' — showing the empty pant legs
jokes.setup: Each new feature of the suit proves more conclusively it's women's clothing
jokes.punchline: Michael helpfully demonstrates the absence of pockets — confirming the indictment
jokes.explanation: The pocket-check escalation is a nice beat in a running sequence. Not a standalone joke but adds to the cumulative comedy of the suit reveal. Michael's helpfulness in demonstrating his own guilt is on-brand.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Negotiations are all about controlling things. About being in the driver's seat. And... you make one tiny mistake, you're dead. I made one tiny mistake. I wore women's clothes.'
jokes.setup: Michael frames the negotiation philosophically
jokes.punchline: The 'tiny mistake' that torpedoed his negotiation was accidentally wearing a women's suit — recast as a negotiation error rather than a personal humiliation
jokes.explanation: The callback structure here is excellent. The serious, analytical framing ('negotiations are all about controlling things') makes the anticlimax of 'I wore women's clothes' land hard. The structure — grand principle, then the specific tiny failure — is textbook and executed well. The economy is superb; it's a perfect talking-head button.

jokes.text: Kevin asks Karen how she feels that Roy tried to 'kick her boyfriend's ass over another woman'
jokes.setup: Karen is calmly recounting the attack story
jokes.punchline: Kevin asks the most awkwardly phrased, socially inappropriate version of the obvious question
jokes.explanation: Kevin's blundering social awareness is well-deployed here. Asking Karen 'how do you feel' that her boyfriend's ex-fiancée's current boyfriend was attacked by the ex — and calling it 'over another woman' — is maximally obtuse. Karen's flat 'I feel great, Kevin. Thank you.' is a perfect non-answer.

jokes.text: Jim to Pam: 'Sorry I almost got you killed.' Pam: 'Yeah. That was nuts.'
jokes.setup: Jim approaches Pam after the violent attack that was partly caused by their complicated relationship
jokes.punchline: Both treat potential murder with complete casual understatement — 'Yeah. That was nuts.'
jokes.explanation: The understatement works — both Jim and Pam dancing around the enormous emotional weight of the situation with 'That was nuts' is very much their dynamic. Understated cringe with emotional resonance.

jokes.text: Jim tells Pam 'I'm sure you guys'll find your way back to one another someday' about her and Roy — deeply passive-aggressive given his feelings
jokes.setup: Pam says her relationship with Roy is completely over
jokes.punchline: Jim — clearly in love with Pam — wishes her well with Roy in a way that is transparently insincere
jokes.explanation: A cringe beat that works emotionally more than comedically — Jim's passive-aggression is visible to everyone except apparently himself. The comedy is in the discomfort, not a punch. Serviceable.

jokes.text: Darryl slides his salary request across the desk; Michael reads it: 'Oh... Come on... be serious.' Darryl: 'I am serious, Mike. That's a 10% raise.'
jokes.setup: Michael uses tactic of writing numbers on paper, expecting a low ask
jokes.punchline: The number is apparently shocking to Michael — a 10% raise request he treats as absurd
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the pay stub reveal to follow. The reaction comedy works but isn't distinguished on its own.

jokes.text: Michael proves his salary by showing his pay stub — Darryl is shocked: 'Mike, this is barely more than I make. You've been here ten years, dog.' Michael: '14 years.'
jokes.setup: Michael claims he can't give Darryl a raise because corporate won't allow it
jokes.punchline: His actual salary is revealed to be barely above a warehouse worker's — after 14 years
jokes.explanation: The pay stub reveal is a genuinely good joke because it's dark — Michael is genuinely pathetic here in a way that transcends comedy. 'You've been here ten years, dog.' / '14 years.' is a tight exchange. The dark undercurrent of Michael's sad professional life makes this funnier and sadder simultaneously.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'A boss's salary isn't just about money. It is about perks. For example, every year, I get a $100 gas card. Can't put a price tag on that.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to put a positive spin on his embarrassingly low salary
jokes.punchline: 'Can't put a price tag on that' — said of a $100 gas card, which has an extremely specific price tag
jokes.explanation: The irony is maximally compressed: 'Can't put a price tag on that' about something that is literally worth exactly $100. Michael's delusion that a $100 gas card compensates for a decade-undersized salary is tragic and funny simultaneously. Clean, efficient, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Toby finds Michael in the parking lot and hands him $15: 'Here's the $15 I owe you. I heard you might need it.' — mocking Michael's salary
jokes.setup: Michael's salary has just been exposed as barely more than a warehouse worker's
jokes.punchline: Toby — the person Michael hates most — appears to pay back $15 with pointed charity, suggesting Michael is now that poor
jokes.explanation: Great dark comedy from the most unexpected source — Toby gets to twist the knife in Michael's worst moment. 'I heard you might need it' lands as the closest Toby gets to a burn. The character integration is strong on both ends — Michael has no good response.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head: 'Yeah, I heard how much Michael makes. I still think he's way overpaid.'
jokes.setup: We know Michael's salary is shockingly low
jokes.punchline: Darryl still thinks it's too much — a double-layered insult
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — eight words deliver maximum damage. We've just been shocked by how little Michael makes, and Darryl's verdict that it's still too much is a beautifully brutal one-liner. The deadpan delivery in a talking head makes it land perfectly. Earns high scores for pure compression.

jokes.text: Darryl tells Michael he needs to get his own raise: 'You gotta call your girl... and get paid. Show her who wears the pants in the relationship.'
jokes.setup: Michael can't give Darryl more than his own salary allows
jokes.punchline: 'Show her who wears the pants' — said to a man who has been wearing women's pants all day
jokes.explanation: This is the best structural joke in the episode. Darryl advises Michael to 'show her who wears the pants' — a common idiom — but we've spent the last several minutes establishing that Michael is literally wearing women's pants. The double meaning is completely organic, completely earned, requires no winking at the camera, and lands as one of those perfect accidental-on-purpose moments. Earns 8+ on all dimensions — originality, structure, character integration, and it's deeply satisfying on rewatch.

jokes.text: That's 'cause of you, Mike. They're not gonna give the working man more than the boss. / Well, what am I supposed to do? / Get your own raise.
jokes.setup: Michael says corporate will only allow a 5% raise for Darryl
jokes.punchline: Darryl explains the logic and the solution in total deadpan: if Michael's cap is too low, Michael needs to raise HIS cap first
jokes.explanation: Darryl's logic is actually correct, which makes it funnier — he out-negotiates the boss in a negotiation about negotiating. Darryl as the most competent person in the room is a great character dynamic.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I am makin' it happen... Sergeant.' — responding to Darryl's 'Make it happen, Captain.'
jokes.setup: Darryl says 'Make it happen, Captain' as encouragement
jokes.punchline: Michael slightly demotes him to 'Sergeant' in his response — the tiniest possible power move
jokes.explanation: A small but efficient joke — Michael's only power move available is a one-rank military demotion in a playful exchange. Characteristically petty and recognizably Michael.

jokes.text: Dwight compares accepting Jim's lunch offer to Han Solo receiving payment for saving the rebel cause
jokes.setup: Jim offers to buy Dwight lunch as thanks
jokes.punchline: Dwight invokes Han Solo and the Death Star as a moral framework for refusing gifts — with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Dwight using Star Wars as moral philosophy is deeply in-character and lands well. The specificity ('the Millennium Falcon,' 'TIE fighters,' 'rebel cause') demonstrates Dwight's complete immersion in the analogy. It also slightly misreads Han Solo, who was notably motivated by reward — which adds another layer.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I've never asked for a raise in 14 years. This is long overdue. I want to do it today.' — immediately after learning his salary is embarrassingly low
jokes.setup: The pay stub humiliation has just occurred
jokes.punchline: Michael's response to learning he's underpaid for 14 years is a burst of sudden motivation, treated as a fresh revelation
jokes.explanation: Serviceable transition beat — Michael's sudden galvanization after 14 years of passivity is funny in a bleak way. Not a strong standalone joke but serves the plot.

jokes.text: Michael to Toby: 'Come on, let's go. I'm gonna smack you in the head with a hammer. Come on, let's go.' — said like a friendly invitation
jokes.setup: Michael reluctantly has to bring Toby to his salary negotiation
jokes.punchline: Michael announces violent intent against Toby in exactly the same tone as 'let's grab coffee'
jokes.explanation: The specific violence ('smack you in the head with a hammer') combined with the cheerful 'Come on, let's go' cadence is a great joke. The mundane delivery of a murder threat is very Michael and scores high on character integration. Toby's presumably resigned 'All right' (implied) makes it better.

jokes.text: Michael quotes Chris Tucker's line from Rush Hour to Darryl — 'Don't ever touch a black man's radio!' — then immediately clarifies he won't touch Darryl's radio
jokes.setup: Michael and Darryl are driving together; Michael presumably touches the radio
jokes.punchline: Michael deploys a movie quote about race as though it's a cultural bonding moment, then assures Darryl he'll respect his radio — the squirming self-consciousness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael racial obliviousness — quoting a movie about race relations as though it's practical relationship advice. The immediate backpedal ('I won't touch yours, by the way') shows Michael's awareness that he's just said something awkward while not understanding why. Good cringe beat.

jokes.text: Michael accidentally ordered 12,000 reams of paper instead of 12 — revealed mid-scene
jokes.setup: Someone reads a report about Michael's recent office decisions
jokes.punchline: Michael ordered 12,000 reams of paper — a quantity that would fill the building — instead of 12
jokes.explanation: A throwaway gag that works as background incompetence comedy. Not especially original but functional.

jokes.text: Darryl coaches Michael before the Jan negotiation: 'Pippity poppity, give me the zoppity.' Michael repeats it enthusiastically.
jokes.setup: Darryl claims to be teaching Michael 'new black man phrases' to help in the negotiation
jokes.punchline: The phrase is complete nonsense — Darryl is pranking Michael, who repeats it with full confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest moments in the episode. Darryl inventing a completely fake 'black man phrase' to trick Michael exploits Michael's racial obliviousness in the most elegant way. The nonsense phrase itself is perfectly constructed nonsense — it sounds almost like it could be something. Michael's enthusiastic 'Yes, sir!' confirms he'll say it in front of Jan. Highly quotable, strong character integration on both ends. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head: 'Yeah. I taught Michael some new phrases. I want him to get the raise. I... just can't help myself.'
jokes.setup: Darryl has just sent Michael into Jan's office with a fake phrase
jokes.punchline: 'I just can't help myself' — Darryl is fully aware he's sabotaging Michael while also genuinely wanting him to succeed
jokes.explanation: The contradiction — 'I want him to get the raise. I just can't help myself.' — is a perfect encapsulation of Darryl's relationship with Michael. He genuinely wants to help but the opportunity to prank Michael is irresistible. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Roy reappears; Kevin shouts 'Roy! Look out!' — then Roy calmly says 'Thanks, Kev. I'm... good, though.'
jokes.setup: Roy has returned peacefully to talk to Pam; Kevin treats him like an ongoing threat
jokes.punchline: Roy's calm, almost embarrassed acknowledgment — 'Thanks, Kev. I'm... good, though.'
jokes.explanation: Good callback beat — Kevin's panic at Roy's return is completely misplaced (Roy is clearly reformed), and Roy's gentle, slightly mortified deflection ('I'm... good, though') is a nice character moment for Roy, showing his own embarrassment about his earlier actions.

jokes.text: Michael says 'Bippity boppity' to Jan in the negotiation — a mangled version of Darryl's fake phrase
jokes.setup: Darryl coached Michael to say 'Pippity poppity, give me the zoppity' in the negotiation
jokes.punchline: Michael actually deploys it — but gets it wrong, saying 'Bippity boppity' instead
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Darryl prank is excellent — but the extra layer of Michael getting the fake phrase wrong ('Bippity boppity' instead of 'Pippity poppity') is the perfect final twist. It suggests Michael practiced a nonsense phrase and still couldn't remember it. Jan's silence in response IS the reaction. This is the episode's best callback, and it earns the score — multilayered, perfectly timed, character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael threatens Jan: 'You give me a good raise, or no more sex.'
jokes.setup: Jan is trying to conduct a professional salary negotiation; Michael is failing tactically
jokes.punchline: Michael inverts the classic power dynamic by leveraging the most inappropriate possible bargaining chip in a professional context
jokes.explanation: The punchline is maximally inappropriate and maximally Michael. The fact that he's threatening to withhold sex from his boss — in a salary negotiation — in front of Toby — is a perfect storm of Michael Scott comedy. Clean, fast, devastating. The economy (seven words of pure cringe) is excellent.

jokes.text: Toby's talking head: 'This may be the first time that a male subordinate has attempted to get a modest, scheduled raise by threatening to withhold sex from a female superior. It will be a groundbreaking case... when it inevitably goes to trial.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just said 'no more sex' to Jan in a salary negotiation
jokes.punchline: Toby — the put-upon HR rep — calmly frames it as an unprecedented legal case, noting with resignation that it 'will inevitably go to trial'
jokes.explanation: Toby's talking head is a highlight of the episode. 'Inevitably goes to trial' is the perfect button — Toby's weary certainty that Michael's behavior will produce a landmark legal case. The clinical framing ('modest, scheduled raise,' 'male subordinate,' 'female superior') contrasted with the absurd situation is exactly Toby's character voice. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Roy apologizes to Pam: 'I just kept thinking about you two together, and I thought you guys were really good friends or... or maybe he was gay or something.' Pause. 'Not that that's wrong.'
jokes.setup: Roy is sincerely apologizing for attacking Jim
jokes.punchline: His justification — he assumed Jim was either just a friend or gay — ends with the classic embarrassed qualifier 'Not that that's wrong'
jokes.explanation: 'Not that that's wrong' is a familiar comedy beat but Roy's delivery in this emotional context makes it funnier than it would be on its own. Works as character comedy — Roy is trying sincerely and still flubbing it.

jokes.text: Jim gives Dwight a fake 'Certificate of Bravery from the Scranton Police Department' — complete with a teddy bear in a policeman's cap
jokes.setup: Dwight has refused all forms of thanks from Jim
jokes.punchline: Jim's workaround is a fake official certificate — which Dwight reads aloud with growing suspicion, noticing the teddy bear graphic
jokes.explanation: Jim's solution to Dwight's gift refusal — a fake official certificate — is creative and perfectly in character for Jim's prankster approach. Dwight reading it aloud ('Recognizing outstanding citizenship from a very brave young man') is funny. The teddy bear detail is a superb visual gag. 'Mm... didn't think you'd notice' confirms Jim made it himself. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Dwight, holding the children's bravery certificate: 'Please, they hand these out to little kids. Look, there's a teddy bear in a policeman's cap.' Jim: 'Mm...didn't think you'd notice.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is pointing out how beneath him the certificate is
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'didn't think you'd notice' admits the trolling — he absolutely expected Dwight to notice
jokes.explanation: Jim's delivery of 'Mm...didn't think you'd notice' is a Jim-camera-look in audio form. The joke is the revealed intent — of course he knew. This is Jim's way of thanking Dwight while maintaining plausible deniability about sincerity. Perfect economy.

jokes.text: Michael's sad litany: 'I accidentally cross-dressed. And then Darryl made me feel bad for not making any money. And then I had to ride up here with stupid Toby.'
jokes.setup: Jan asks Michael what's wrong before the negotiation
jokes.punchline: Michael summarizes the day as a list of cascading indignities, each one worse than the last, delivered with the resignation of a man who has simply had enough
jokes.explanation: 'I accidentally cross-dressed' as an opening of a complaint list is a near-perfect line. 'Accidentally' is doing so much work. The escalation from the suit to financial humiliation to Toby (the final indignity) is well-structured. The callback function — compressing the entire episode's subplots — makes this a satisfying chapter-close.

jokes.text: Jan coaches Michael to ask for 15% so she can say no and give 12%: 'I just need you to ask for it... so I can record that you asked for it.'
jokes.setup: Michael is being coached on how to conduct his own salary negotiation — by the person on the other side of it
jokes.punchline: Jan is orchestrating a fake negotiation where she pre-determines the outcome and just needs Michael to play along
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurdity of Jan coaching Michael to negotiate against her — the performance of negotiation rather than negotiation itself. Michael's naive compliance ('Ah, so... All right, Levinson. I would like a 15% raise.') is funny. Works as a commentary on corporate theater.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I would like a 15% raise.' Jan: 'No! But we can offer you 12.' Michael: 'But you just said 15.' Jan: 'Negotiation is an art.'
jokes.setup: Jan has just told Michael to ask for 15% so she can say no and offer 12%
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately calls Jan out — 'But you just said 15' — and Jan responds with the breezy 'Negotiation is an art,' treating the theater as legitimate
jokes.explanation: 'Negotiation is an art' as a dismissal of Michael catching her in the pretense is a good button. Jan's breeziness about the entire charade is on-brand for her character's relationship with Michael.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: 'Both Darryl and I took something. Higher salaries. Win, win, win.'
jokes.setup: Michael is summarizing the outcome of the day's negotiations
jokes.punchline: 'Win, win, win' — Michael's signature three-win formula applied to a situation where he performed almost no actual negotiation
jokes.explanation: The 'Win, win, win' is a recurring Michael Scott verbal tic that lands well here because it's applied to a negotiation Michael completely fumbled. The extra 'win' (three instead of the standard two) is Michael's signature excess.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head continues: 'But, you know, life is about more than just salary. It's about... perks. Like having sex with Jan.' Jan, off-camera: 'Michael!'
jokes.setup: Michael is wrapping up his philosophical summary about what salary means
jokes.punchline: He lists 'having sex with Jan' as a professional perk — in a talking head — apparently in Jan's presence
jokes.explanation: Jan's off-camera 'Michael!' is the perfect button — she's apparently in the room during his talking head confession. The joke works because Michael is so committed to his enumeration of perks that he includes something completely inappropriate. The structure (serious list → absurd final entry → caught) is clean.

jokes.text: Dwight reads bravery stories to Angela in her office; she suggests they read it together; both exchange loaded looks
jokes.setup: Dwight enters Angela's office with 'very interesting reading' about bravery
jokes.punchline: The wooden, almost spy-coded exchange — 'I was thinking tonight, we could... read it together.' 'That sounds... fun.' — is their secret romance played as absurd formality
jokes.explanation: The Dwight/Angela secret romance coded as extremely stilted formal conversation is a consistent show joke. 'Reading it together' is clearly a euphemism and both of them know it; the comedy is in the forced plainness of their dialogue trying to hide something obvious. Works especially on rewatch knowing their relationship.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head about the fake certificate: 'I... will never say a word. And now... we are even.'
jokes.setup: Jim has given Dwight a fake police certificate; Dwight apparently accepted it without exposing it as fake
jokes.punchline: Jim's solemn, pause-laden declaration of a truce — 'we are even' — treated with the gravity of a peace treaty
jokes.explanation: The resolution of the Jim/Dwight thread is handled beautifully. 'We are even' with gravitas — for a life-debt settled by a fake certificate — is perfect. The pauses in the line ('I... will never say a word. And now... we are even.') do real comedic work, matching the mock-solemnity of the moment.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I graduated from anger management the same way I graduated from Cornell... on time. Now I'm back, got a second chance, and I'm not gonna blow it. So look out, Dunder-Mifflin!'
jokes.setup: Andy returns from anger management and delivers a triumphant returning-champion speech
jokes.punchline: 'Look out, Dunder-Mifflin!' — then immediately: 'I mean look out in a fun way. Not like I'm gonna hurt you.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's immediate self-correction of 'look out' is a near-perfect joke structure. The setup is a triumphant comeback speech; the punchline is that his language immediately raises alarm bells he has to defuse — demonstrating that anger management has made him MORE self-aware but not less volatile. The Cornell brag ('the same way I graduated from Cornell... on time') adds a perfect character note. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Andy walks back into the office saying 'Hey, guys! Guess who's back?' — multiple people scream and recoil in fear
jokes.setup: Andy has just finished a speech about not being threatening
jokes.punchline: His colleagues immediately prove the opposite — they're terrified of him — undercutting his entire speech in real time
jokes.explanation: The structure is impeccable: Andy says 'I mean look out in a fun way, not like I'm gonna hurt you' — then immediately everyone screams when he enters. It's the physical proof that his reassurance was necessary and insufficient. The juxtaposition between talking head and scene is the classic mockumentary format working at its best.

jokes.text: Dwight, reacting to the office screaming at Andy's return: 'No need to thank me. I am not a hero. I am a mere defender of the office. You know who's a real hero? Hiro from Heroes. That's a hero. Also Bono.'
jokes.setup: Dwight earlier refused the 'hero' label with an elaborate speech about real heroes; now the chaos of Andy's return triggers another declaration
jokes.punchline: His revised list of 'real heroes' is 'Hiro from Heroes' (a pun on his own name) and 'Also Bono' — completely arbitrary additions delivered with Dwight's characteristic authority
jokes.explanation: The episode's funniest moment and a near-perfect closer. Callbacks the earlier 'real heroes are superheroes' speech, then upgrades it: 'Hiro from Heroes' is a perfect pun (and the show Heroes was at peak cultural moment), and 'Also Bono' is the funniest possible arbitrary third option. The 'Also Bono' construction — no explanation, no connection, just Bono — is comedy gold. Dwight's complete sincerity ties it together. Justifies high scores on originality, character integration, and earned — this is all built on the episode's own architecture. One of the show's great Dwight moments.

tmdb_overview: Roy paced in the parking lot outside Dunder-Mifflin and then charged the building looking for Jim. When he spots Jim and rushed him, only to get pepper sprayed in the eyes by Dwight, who managed to spray everybody around him, as well.
